strengths: The paper addresses an important question: whether optimization methods that improve generalization can also increase membership leakage. The reported single-query results provide useful evidence that these outcomes can coexist.

The evaluation covers four image and tabular datasets, several attack methods, and additional image-model architectures. Reporting means and standard deviations across five randomized runs strengthens the empirical presentation.

SharpReg is a simple modification requiring one target model and demonstrates substantial reductions in measured attack accuracy. On CIFAR-100, single-query accuracy falls from 76.68% to 59.64%, while test accuracy falls from 79.92% to 75.86%.
weaknesses: The central influence-entropy metric is not mathematically well-defined as presented. Influence scores can be negative, so normalization in Equation (3) does not necessarily produce probabilities. Appendix C.1 also assigns 2,153 examples with entirely zero influence vectors to the highest-entropy bucket, although Equation (3) yields an undefined normalization. Explicit handling of these cases and sensitivity analysis are necessary to validate the resulting memorization spectrum.

The proposed memorization mechanism is supported only indirectly. The buckets use precomputed SGD influence scores on CIFAR-100; memorization is not re-estimated under SAM or SWA. Improved accuracy within these buckets therefore does not establish increased memorization. Differences in example difficulty and accuracy headroom provide alternative explanations, particularly because the highest bucket approaches an accuracy ceiling. Direct memorization measurements and links to individual examples' membership leakage are missing.

SharpReg's claimed additional anti-overfitting mechanism is not isolated. For xi < 1, Equation (5) equals Equation (4) with lambda replaced by lambda/(1-xi), multiplied by the positive constant (1-xi). Thus, subtracting xi times the training loss introduces no independent objective component beyond changing the sharpness tradeoff and optimization scale. Appendix C.4.1 acknowledges parameter redundancy, but the interpretation and ablations still require controls matching effective lambda, learning rate, and weight decay.

The privacy conclusions are broader than the observations. In Table 1, SAM reduces multi-query attack accuracy on CIFAR-100 from 69.18% to 65.41% and on CIFAR-10 from 56.36% to 54.01%; the additional architectures show the same reversal. Purchase-100's single-query increase is small relative to the reported variability. These findings warrant a more qualified, attack-specific conclusion. A fixed SAM radius and absent measurements of achieved sharpness also limit attribution to flatness itself.

The security evaluation lacks stronger sample-specific attacks such as LiRA and reports only attack accuracy, without ROC curves or true-positive rates at low false-positive rates. Consequently, it does not establish whether SharpReg protects the most vulnerable examples or whether the privacy ordering persists under stronger attacks.

The attack reporting contains an important inconsistency. For balanced membership evaluation, Equation (8) and Table 4's CIFAR-100 SGD training/test accuracies imply correctness-attack accuracy around 59.84%, whereas Table 3 reports 77.04%. Different evaluation halves do not readily explain this discrepancy. The actual member/nonmember counts, balancing procedure, and table entries need reconciliation before the evaluation can be confidently interpreted.

SharpReg's comparative advantage remains insufficiently demonstrated. SELENA achieves both higher test accuracy and lower attack accuracy than the principal SharpReg configuration on CIFAR-100 and Texas-100 in Table 4. Comparisons against tuned early stopping and ordinary regularization at matched utility are needed to isolate the benefit of encouraging sharpness. Runtime and memory measurements would also substantiate the claimed efficiency advantage.
